items.text: Golden Wattle pays a Meowfia +3 no matter who they bond with. Cats offered handshakes to everyone, and Farm quickly learned that an offer is a tell (Blair, Finley). Make it a risk for cats too, for example -3 to a Meowfia who bonds with Farm when Farm wins the round.

items.text: Golden Wattle handshakes are public and immediate, so offering one gives away your read. Only the Meowfia used it, and it rewarded a losing team with +3 each. Fix: make bonds secret until round end, or pay the Meowfia bonus only if their side wins.

items.text: Crimson Kunzea is too swingy. Doubled wins were most of every final score, and in round 3 four Farm players doubled down on an obvious read. Consider a cap (for example, +50% value) or limit it to one player per round.
items.title: The Hawk Speaks Twice

items.text: Crimson Kunzea is too strong and too early. Five players doubled in round 2 and all six in round 3, mostly before the evidence was in. Votes locked publicly, and the talk turned into arithmetic like 'Blair goes regardless'. Fix: allow doubling only after you have spoken once, or cap the bonus at your highest card.
items.title: The Mouser's Three Winks

items.text: Blair (would change): I'd tone down Crimson Kunzea. Doubling the whole round score for committing early rewards being first to slam the table more than actually reasoning things out, and it swung the standings more than anything else.

items.text: Wink plus Crimson Kunzea: a player who doubled down has committed their votes publicly, so a single Wink can erase them all (Ellis's 6). One action swung the game. Consider letting committed double-down votes count even if the thrower dies afterwards.
items.title: The Third Cat

items.text: Crimson Kunzea was never used. It has to be done before your first message, which is too early to know anything. Allow it any time before you've accused someone, or before the CAW opens.

items.text: Crimson Kunzea was revealed in both rounds, and nobody ever doubled down. You must commit before you have spoken, while the bonus only pays if you are right, so it never looks worth the risk. Let players double down later in the day, or give a reason to do it blind.

items.text: Chicken and the consolation rule both reward losing cats too cheaply. A House Cat learns who the Chicken is and zeroes them with one card, which then comes back as consolation (Casey lost a 26-point throw). A cat that knows it is losing can throw one card at any Farm player and get it back, as Blair and Ellis both did.

items.text: Round 2 had one Meowfia and scores swung 14 points on one throw, so the leader decides the game. Consider capping banked values or catch-up rules.
items.title: The Floofer Confession

items.text: Alex (would change): I'd make the dawn reports clearer about who visited whom, so players can cross-check claims without guessing at egg-payment rules.
items.title: The Floofer Confession

items.text: Ellis (would change): I would make it clearer which animal pays the visitor and which pays the visited player, since that one rule decided most of the arguments.

items.title: The Floofer Confession

items.text: Farm eggsecuted a Farm player in two of three rounds with weak evidence. Group pile-ons on whoever changed a claim, even honestly, favour Meowfia too much.
items.title: Rules Lawyers and Wild Cards

items.text: Meowfia doubled stakes plus 5 points make the winning cats run away with the score. Alex reached 49 from one throw, and Blair at 11 had no path to winning. Consider capping the double or the round bonus.
items.title: Rules Lawyers and Wild Cards

items.text: Silence is cheap: Alex stayed quiet for most of rounds 1 and 2 and was never suspected. Consider a rule that rewards or forces a claim.
items.title: Rules Lawyers and Wild Cards

items.text: Blair (would change): Make the role and visit reports easier to check, such as showing each player's visitors, so claims can be verified instead of argued.
items.title: Rules Lawyers and Wild Cards

items.text: Ellis (would change): Make dawn reports say explicitly whose visits are being counted, so players don't have to reason through the rule text in public.
items.title: Rules Lawyers and Wild Cards

items.text: The leader Ellis was never threatened, with no catch-up pressure. Rounds 2 and 3 were easy Farm wins, so third place was already decided. Consider a rubber-band bonus for trailing players.
items.title: The Turkey Takes All

items.text: Meowfia don't know each other and had little to do. Drew threw at a Farm player in round 2 to no effect, and Blair was a lone Meowfia in round 3 who was quickly caught. Give them a stronger bluffing tool.
items.title: The Turkey Takes All

items.text: The two-step vote barely changed anything. The CAW CAW calls decided the vote, and the finger-pointing step never showed in the log.
items.title: The Turkey Takes All

items.text: Alex (would change): I'd make the dawn report name the visitor's role or the target's role, so players can check claims without guessing.
items.title: The Turkey Takes All

items.text: Casey (would change): I'd make the dawn report name each visitor or payout source, so players can check claims without guessing from egg counts. That would cut down on the mismatches that drove most of the accusations.
items.title: The Turkey Takes All

items.text: Drew (would change): I would make the Storyteller's dawn reports say which animal visited whom, so players have less room to claim roles that can't be checked.
items.title: The Turkey Takes All

items.text: The Confused status reads as a lie. Finley's report was wrong, nobody could separate it from deceit, and a Farm player was eggsecuted. Give the confused player a way to be checked, or tell the table that someone was confused.
items.title: Floofer Walks Into Daylight

items.text: The AI players kept confusing role re-dealing with role swapping, and cited past rounds' claims. Print each round's roles as new, or tell the table clearly that roles reset.
items.title: Floofer Walks Into Daylight

items.text: The 4-beat day was repetitive. Players restated the same question and many beats added nothing. The eggsecution target was fixed by beat 2 in rounds 1 and 3. Consider fewer beats or more private information to bluff with.
items.title: Floofer Walks Into Daylight

items.text: Alex (would change): I'd have the Storyteller state the visitors and the hug status in every dawn report, so players can verify claims without guessing.
items.title: Floofer Walks Into Daylight

items.text: Casey (would change): I would make the day less dependent on claimed roles with no proof, since a single confused or dishonest report could decide an eggsecution.
items.title: Floofer Walks Into Daylight

items.text: Drew (would change): Make dawn reports spell out what each role learned, including blank or confused results, so players can check claims instead of guessing.
items.title: Floofer Walks Into Daylight

items.text: Ellis (would change): Tell each player whether a visit to them was hugged or confused in their dawn report, so null results can be judged instead of misread. Also make it clearer which visits were blocked or hugged.
items.title: Floofer Walks Into Daylight

items.text: Finley (would change): Let confused players see a clearer flag that their report is unreliable, so the table doesn't treat a confused egg count as solid evidence.
items.title: Floofer Walks Into Daylight

items.text: Alex, round 3: Called the Blair and Finley role changes a swap, though roles are re-dealt each round. Blair had to correct this.
items.title: Floofer Walks Into Daylight

items.text: Double-value banking on Farm throws from Meowfia is far too strong. Drew's 46 and 40 point rounds decided the whole game by round 1. Cap the bank, or stop doubling when most of the table throws at the same target.
items.title: The Drew Show

items.text: Round scores dwarf the 5-point team bonus, so winning the round matters far less than the size of the throw. Cut stake values or raise the bonus.
items.title: The Drew Show

items.text: With ties going to Farm and the table piling onto one name, the votes never felt in doubt. Rounds 1 and 3 were decided by a single dubious claim chased by everyone.
items.title: The Drew Show

items.text: Blair (would change): Make the dawn reports say who visited you when a hug or visit lands, so claims can be checked instead of argued.
items.title: The Drew Show

items.text: Finley, round 1: Said four players visited Casey and that Casey should gain eggs. Later claimed Casey should be +1 from visiting Drew.
items.title: The Drew Show

items.text: Confused made Farm players look guilty twice (Blair round 1, Alex round 2). Both were eggsecuted with no real evidence. Consider telling a confused player which stat is wrong, or making this less lethal.
items.title: Eggs for the Wrong Basket

items.text: Meowfia won two rounds by staying quiet while Farm convicted one of its own. Unexplained eggs act as an automatic scapegoat, so deduction is thin. Consider giving every round some solid checkable evidence.
items.title: Eggs for the Wrong Basket

items.text: Scores are hugely lopsided. Banking a few high cards in one winning round (Casey +14, Ellis +11) decided the game, so round 3 outweighed rounds 1 and 2. Consider capping banked values or scaling them.
items.title: Eggs for the Wrong Basket

items.text: Players invented claims that other facts quickly disproved, and the dialogue was repetitive. Most turns just restated 'who gave Alex the +2?' without new info. Consider fewer beats or a prompt that forces new information.
items.title: Eggs for the Wrong Basket

items.text: Alex (would change): Flag confused players' reports as unreliable in the day summary, or give the table visit counts so claims can be checked without guessing.
items.title: Eggs for the Wrong Basket

items.text: Blair (confused by): Confused reports made the dawn information hard to trust, since I couldn't tell whether my egg-gain story was real or a confusion artifact. It also wasn't clear which visits were reliable when several players gave conflicting claims.
items.title: Eggs for the Wrong Basket

items.text: Blair (would change): I'd make dawn reports show the confusion more clearly, so players know which of their own information to discount.
items.title: Eggs for the Wrong Basket

items.text: Casey (confused by): The dawn reports were hard to trust, since confused players got wrong egg counts and animals, so I couldn't tell which claims were real.
items.title: Eggs for the Wrong Basket

items.text: Casey (would change): Make confused reports clearer, so players can tell which numbers and roles to trust without guessing.
items.title: Eggs for the Wrong Basket

items.text: Drew (confused by): The rule about how many Meowfia there are per round and whether Meowfia can recognize each other was hard to track. I couldn't tell whether a teammate was at the table, so I misjudged Blair.
items.title: Eggs for the Wrong Basket

items.text: Drew (would change): I'd let Meowfia players learn who their teammates are, so they can coordinate instead of guessing.
items.title: Eggs for the Wrong Basket

items.text: Finley (would change): Make confused players' reports less ambiguous, or show everyone which players are confused, so a single wrong report doesn't drag the whole day.
items.title: Eggs for the Wrong Basket

items.text: Meowfia lost all three rounds, and Blair was eggsecuted every time. With 2 cats among 6 and a majority vote, Farm wins easily. Consider giving Meowfia more tools, or a bonus for surviving a round.
items.title: Blair Always Loses

items.text: Day talk was repetitive and converged early. Most players just agreed with each other and called CAW. The 4-beat structure with few real conflicts gave little tension.
items.title: Blair Always Loses

items.text: Cats rarely used their night information well. Casey and Drew often threw nothing or stayed quiet, and no Meowfia stake ever banked, so Meowfia scored almost nothing. The 2x Meowfia stake is irrelevant in practice.
items.title: Blair Always Loses

items.text: Casey (would change): Print the exact wording of each animal's ability in the dawn report, or let players check the rule text, so visit-counting disputes stop turning on memory.
items.title: Blair Always Loses

items.text: Dead players' cards count for nothing as votes but can still bank points. A Wink on an accuser removes votes and costs the Meowfia nothing. Consider capping or nerfing the Wink, or announcing a timed death.
items.title: The Tied Throw

items.text: Standings barely shaped play. Nobody treated leader Alex differently, and Farm teammates fed him wins. The first-round bank of 15 made him a runaway leader. Consider a cap on banked points per round, or a catch-up bonus.
items.title: The Tied Throw

items.text: The Farm threw 6+ votes on one suspect each round, so rounds were decided by conformity, not by evidence. Late-day votes drifted to whoever was loudest.
items.title: The Tied Throw

items.text: Alex (would change): I'd make the dawn reports clearer about which nest changes came from which visitor, so players can check claims faster.
items.title: The Tied Throw

items.text: Blair (would change): Dawn reports could state who visited each player, not just the egg count, so players wouldn't have to reconstruct visits from nest sizes.
items.title: The Tied Throw

items.text: Casey (would change): Put each visitor's identity or the source of each egg in the dawn report, so players can check claims directly instead of reasoning from nest counts.
items.title: The Tied Throw

items.text: Drew (would change): Make the dawn reports clearer about confusion, so a confused player's report isn't just a vague warning that can't be checked.
items.title: The Tied Throw

items.text: Ellis (would change): I would make the nest-change reports clearer, such as stating each visitor's role effect, so players spend less time reconciling claims.
items.title: The Tied Throw

items.text: Finley (would change): I would make the dawn reports clearer about who visited whom, so players can cross-check claims without guessing at animal rules.
items.title: The Tied Throw

items.text: Drew, round 1: Kept asking who took his egg after noting that he was confused. His -1 was a false confused report.
items.title: The Tied Throw

items.text: Finley, round 2: Said Alex's unchanged nest proved Blair never visited. Retracted it later.
items.title: The Tied Throw

items.text: Alex, round 3: Said Casey's unchanged nest meant somebody visited her. A visit does not have to change a nest.
items.title: The Tied Throw

items.text: The Farm side won rounds by group-think, not clean deduction. Claims were rarely checkable, and players followed the loudest accuser.
items.title: Turkey Rules Confusion

items.text: Scores snowballed: Finley led from round 1 and kept first even after losing round 3. Catch-up for trailing players is weak, and Ellis ended at 3 points.
items.title: Turkey Rules Confusion

items.text: Alex (would change): I'd make the dawn reports name visitors more clearly, so players can check each other's claims without relying on flat-nest arithmetic that is easy to misread.
items.title: Turkey Rules Confusion

items.text: Blair (would change): Dawn reports should name the visitors when the role allows it, so claims can be checked more reliably. Right now it's hard to tell who is lying when reports stay vague.
items.title: Turkey Rules Confusion

items.text: Drew (confused by): The confusion rule was hard to track: a confused dawn report can be wrong about your egg count and your learned role, so I couldn't tell which of my Round 3 reads to trust.
items.title: Turkey Rules Confusion

items.text: Drew (would change): I'd make the dawn reports name the visitors when a role learns them, so players aren't left guessing whether a visit happened.
items.title: Turkey Rules Confusion

items.text: Alex, round 3: Treated Casey's and Ellis's visit claims as contradictory when they were not.
items.title: Turkey Rules Confusion

items.text: Runaway leader: round 1 gave Blair 24 points from three throws, and no one could catch up. The top throw rewards may be too large relative to the 1-to-13 spread. Cap banked cards per round or make a loss cost more.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Farm threw almost only low cards and Wilds, and Meowfia threw high. The 'keep high cards' advice makes Farm play timidly, and the rewards for a Farm win seem small.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Wink kills the dead player's talk but not their throw, so killing a leader does not stop them from scoring. Consider that dead players' throws score at a reduced rate.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Players in a group tended to copy each other's CAW calls and pile on one suspect. Day beats offered little new information, and the tension was low.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Drew (would change): I would make role claims public and checkable, so a lie about a visit exposes itself faster. Right now a single fake egg report can carry a whole round.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Ellis (would change): I would make role claims harder to fake or shift between rounds, so players can't reinvent their roles. I would also show the table which animals visited whom, not just counts.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Finley (confused by): The two-step vote was hard to track: the day-end pointing sets the trial pair, but the pointing and throws are separate, so a dead player's throws still show up without votes. Dead players also kept throwing cards, which I didn't expect.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Finley (would change): I'd make the Storyteller's dawn reports clearer about who visited whom, since several claims in every round were hard to check against each other.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Round 1's 38-point swing from one 2x bank decided the whole game. Cap the bank, or lower the multiplier, so later rounds can matter.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: The leader was never targeted. Blair at 46 points was hard to spot because scores are only announced at the start of rounds, and nobody acted on it. Consider more visible standings.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Alex (confused by): The confused-report mechanic was hard to trust: I couldn't tell whether my own dawn info was wrong, so every visit claim was shaky. Tracking who-visited-whom across claims was also tangled.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Alex (would change): Make dawn reports say whether a visit was to you or from you, so players can check claims faster. Also make the Wink's target clearer, since I accidentally targeted my own name in round 2.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Blair (would change): State the banking and Grudge rules once, clearly, and keep them the same every round so players can plan their throws.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Finley (would change): I would make dawn reports list who visited a player when the role depends on it, so visit claims are easier to check. Ellis's collapse also had no visible cause, which I'd like explained at the table.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Alex, round 2: Named himself as the wink target instead of Ellis, so the Wink was wasted or unclear.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Blair, round 3: Opened with 'Blair's gone', which is an odd self-reference that doesn't fit the game.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Blair, round 3: Thought a Farm stake banks only if the target is Meowfia, and ignored how cats score.
items.title: The Blair Runaway

items.text: Round 1 and round 3 convicted Farm players on mechanical noise. Confusion and hugs left clean-looking reports, so honest players got blamed. Consider telling players when they were hugged, or give them a clue.
items.title: Casey Wins Quietly

items.text: Players only needed to follow the majority. Almost nobody tested the leading suspect in rounds 1 and 3, so the vote converged without checking.
items.title: Casey Wins Quietly

items.text: Scoring rewards a lone Meowfia too heavily. Casey won with a 3-point throw and no pressure. Winners' scores are low, so the first-place race hinged on being Meowfia in the right round.
items.title: Casey Wins Quietly

items.text: Alex (would change): I'd make the dawn reports clearer about who visited whom, so the table can check claims without guessing.
items.title: Casey Wins Quietly

items.text: Blair (would change): Show each player's role and visit targets in the dawn report so claims could be checked against the actual interactions, not inferred from egg counts.
items.title: Casey Wins Quietly

items.text: Drew (would change): I would make the dawn reports clearer about which visits gave eggs and which didn't, so players stop disputing the rules.
items.title: Casey Wins Quietly

items.text: Finley (would change): Make the Storyteller report each visitor's identity to the visited player when eggs are gained, so the table can check claims without guessing.
items.title: Casey Wins Quietly

items.text: Meowfia lost all three rounds. They don't know each other, so they can't coordinate, and the table always finds one target. Consider giving Meowfia a way to learn each other, or a stronger bluff tool.
items.title: Farm Sweeps, Blair Banks

items.text: Everyone throws at the same player every round. Votes are consensus, not hidden decisions, so tension is low. Meowfia teammates even threw at each other (Alex at Blair in round 2).
items.title: Farm Sweeps, Blair Banks

items.text: Players kept low cards and Wilds, so one King throw decided the winner. Winning rounds is not much of a contest. Try a smaller payoff for banking big cards, or a cost to keeping nests large.
items.title: Farm Sweeps, Blair Banks

items.text: Alex (confused by): Round 2's eggsecution was hard to follow: as Meowfia I didn't know Blair was my teammate, so I threw at a teammate and was on the losing side without knowing it. Meowfia not knowing each other makes it easy to hurt your own side.
items.title: Farm Sweeps, Blair Banks

items.text: Alex (would change): Tell each Meowfia player who their teammates are, or at least how many Meowfia there are, so they don't waste throws on their own side.
items.title: Farm Sweeps, Blair Banks

items.text: Blair (would change): I'd make it clearer when a claimed visit can't be verified, since many claims rested on dawn reports that could be wrong. A public nest-change log for each visit would help.
items.title: Farm Sweeps, Blair Banks

items.text: Casey (would change): I'd make the dawn reports say whether a visit was blocked or hugged, so players can tell a missing visit from a false claim.
items.title: Farm Sweeps, Blair Banks

items.text: Ellis (confused by): The Meowfia-side rules were hard to track: I couldn't tell who my partner was, so my round 1 throw at Blair was actually against my own teammate. Hugged players' visits also weren't clearly reported.
items.title: Farm Sweeps, Blair Banks

items.text: Ellis (would change): I'd make the Meowfia partner identity clearer, or at least say which players share the Meowfia side, so teammates aren't forced into blind throws.
items.title: Farm Sweeps, Blair Banks

items.text: Finley (would change): Make dawn reports show the visitor's animal, so players can test each other's claims without guessing.
items.title: Farm Sweeps, Blair Banks

items.text: Doubled banking for Meowfia plus +5 made round 1 worth about 90 points, while later rounds paid about 3 to 21. The score swing from round 1 decided the whole game, so rounds 2 and 3 had no tension. Fix: cap the double or scale it, or cap stake value.
items.title: The Kingmaker Round

items.text: Casey and Finley won round 1 by simply joining the likely mob vote. Meowfia has no need to hide when Farm piles on a random target. A Farm player's wrong accusation has no penalty, so bandwagons are cheap.
items.title: The Kingmaker Round

items.text: Hug and Wink effects hide the source, so Farm cannot check anything. Ellis's triple hug in round 3 left nothing to deduce, and the winks removed Farm voices without changing outcomes.
items.title: The Kingmaker Round

items.text: Players cited roles from past rounds as evidence, though roles are re-dealt. Blair, as Meowfia, was a cheap and consistent scapegoat, and teammates threw nothing at their own partner. Ellis's refusal to stake cost nothing, so partner-sacrifice play is weakly punished.
items.title: The Kingmaker Round

items.text: Alex (would change): I would make the egg and visit reports clearer, so each role's dawn result is easier to check against the nest changes without re-reading the rules.
items.title: The Kingmaker Round

items.text: Casey (would change): I'd make the dawn reports clearer about who visited whom, since many accounts contradicted each other and it was hard to tell who was lying.
items.title: The Kingmaker Round

items.text: Ellis (would change): I'd make the Meowfia partner reveal less confusing: right now Meowfia can't tell who their partner is in a way that lets them coordinate their throws without a lot of guessing.
items.title: The Kingmaker Round

items.text: Finley (would change): I would make hugs and blocked visits more visible at dawn, so players could tell whether a claim was hugged or simply empty. That would cut down on the wrong accusations.
items.title: The Kingmaker Round

items.text: Alex, round 3: Used Blair's role claims from earlier rounds as evidence, though roles are re-dealt every round.
items.title: The Kingmaker Round

items.text: Round 1 scored one lone Meowfia 15 points, while the Farm gained nothing for a mistake. The lone-Meowfia payoff snowballed. Consider capping banked points or giving the team an incentive.
items.title: Casey's Early Lead

items.text: Scoring let early leaders coast. Casey's 17 after round 1 made later rounds nearly irrelevant for the win. Add a comeback mechanism.
items.title: Casey's Early Lead

items.text: Alex (would change): Publish each player's visit targets and claimed roles in one place at the start of the day, so claims can be checked against the nest changes more easily.
items.title: Casey's Early Lead

items.text: Blair (would change): Publish each player's exact visit list and target egg changes in the day summary, so claims could be checked without guessing from nest counts.
items.title: Casey's Early Lead

items.text: Casey (would change): I'd make the dawn reports clearer about who visited whom, since the same gain can come from being visited or from visiting, and that caused most of the confusion.
items.title: Casey's Early Lead

items.text: Drew (would change): I'd make the dawn reports say which player (not just the count) caused each egg change, so visit-and-gain claims are easier to verify.
items.title: Casey's Early Lead

items.text: Ellis (would change): I'd have dawn reports name each visitor and visit target, so claims could be checked against exact nest changes instead of inferred from counts.
items.title: Casey's Early Lead

items.text: Finley (would change): Make the dawn report clearer about who visited you and whether you were confused, so visit claims are easier to check. Otherwise it's hard to separate honest reports from lies.
items.title: Casey's Early Lead

items.text: The 2x Meowfia bank is too swingy. One win let Drew jump from 17 to 77 and decided the whole game. Cap the doubling, or limit how many cards a Meowfia stake can bank.
items.title: The Wink Parade

items.text: The vote is a pile-on. In rounds 1 and 2 the cat was voted out by three or more players, and the Meowfia mostly threw nothing, so the stakes were low. Late-round stakes rarely mattered for Farm.
items.title: The Wink Parade

items.text: Alex (would change): Make the dawn report say who visited you when a visit lands on you (or at least which animal), so visit-based claims can be checked instead of argued.
items.title: The Wink Parade

items.text: Casey (would change): Give each player a way to check visits, such as an egg count that shows who visited, so the day rests on evidence rather than unverifiable claims.
items.title: The Wink Parade

items.text: Drew (would change): I would make the role reports clearer about who visited whom, so players can verify claims instead of arguing from hugs and silence.
items.title: The Wink Parade

items.text: Ellis (would change): I would make dawn reports say who visited you when an egg changes, so players can check claims instead of guessing from nest counts.
items.title: The Wink Parade

items.text: Players followed the first plausible consensus and threw cheap Wilds, so the vote rarely tested anything. Throws of 0 or 1 card showed no confidence, and the 'Ties go to Meowfia' rule gave little reason to commit.
items.title: Casey Takes the Fall

items.text: Casey (would change): Show the learned role and any confusion explicitly in every dawn report, so players can check claims without guessing whether the report is wrong.
items.title: Casey Takes the Fall

items.text: Drew (would change): I'd make the nest-change and egg-gain rules clearer, with a quick reminder of who pays whom for each role. The day would also move faster with fewer contradictory claims.
items.title: Casey Takes the Fall

items.text: Finley (would change): I'd make the dawn report state explicitly who paid an egg and why, so visitor-based egg changes are easier to verify.
items.title: Casey Takes the Fall

items.text: Casey, round 1: Claimed her report showed no role for Blair. The visit was hugged, so she learned nothing, but she called it unreliable and then blamed the missing confusion.
items.title: Casey Takes the Fall

items.text: The Wink is too strong. It killed the only verified Farm read and Ellis scored 17. Consider letting the dead voice a last word, or a cost for winking.
items.title: Wrong Hawk, Lost Eagle

items.text: Scores snowball. Blair led after a lucky round 1, and the final standings follow that. Late-game catch-up is weak because throws can bank very high cards, so big throws at a lucky win dominate.
items.title: Wrong Hawk, Lost Eagle

items.text: Blair (would change): I would make dawn reports state which visits paid eggs, so players can check claims without reconstructing the arithmetic.

items.title: Wrong Hawk, Lost Eagle

items.title: Wrong Hawk, Lost Eagle

items.text: Tension is low. Farm won rounds 2 and 3 with a clear consensus and little doubt, and the vote and trial steps added little.
items.title: Winks and Wrong Eagles

items.text: Dead players still throw and score, so winks have little cost to the victim. Casey's wink in round 3 barely hurt her. Consider limiting scoring for dead players.
items.title: Winks and Wrong Eagles

items.text: Alex (would change): I'd make the dawn reports clearer about which visits landed on your nest, so public counts can settle claims faster.

items.text: Blair (would change): Make it easier to track which visits each player reported, such as a short public log of visits and egg changes, so claims are easier to check.

items.text: Ellis (would change): I'd have dawn reports list each visitor by name and animal, so players can't hide behind vague counts and the table can check claims directly.
