items.text: Score swings are huge. Blair banked 22 in round 2 by throwing a 13, which decided the game after one round. Fix: cap the value a player can bank, or reduce the High-card payoff.
items.title: Wink and Wrong Rules

items.text: Meowfia never lose here: they won 3 of 3 rounds. Farm throws at a plausible target with no hard evidence, and the vote leans on who sounds smooth. Consider giving Farm more checkable info.
items.title: Wink and Wrong Rules

items.text: Dead Finley and early CAW calls cut debate short. The day ended in round 3 with Blair never really getting a fair hearing. Fix: raise the CAW threshold or require a full beat first.
items.title: Wink and Wrong Rules

items.text: Alex (would change): Make the dawn reports more explicit about who visited whom, so players can check claims without guessing at role mechanics. Right now the counts alone leave too much room for honest mistakes to look like lies.
items.title: Wink and Wrong Rules

items.text: Casey (would change): I'd make the dawn reports name the visitors or the target explicitly, so players aren't guessing which egg came from which visit.
items.title: Wink and Wrong Rules

items.text: Drew (would change): I would make the dawn reports show exactly what each role learned, so players can check each other's claims without guessing.
items.title: Wink and Wrong Rules

items.text: The runaway lead is decisive. Finley's 19-point round made rounds 3 irrelevant for first place. Cap the banked value per round, or reduce the cards a player can bank.
items.title: The Wasted Wink

items.text: Throws are mostly Wilds and low cards, so the vote is rarely costly. Round 1 and 3 throws had no real stakes. Raise the minimum throw or the value of the cards returned to the nest.
items.title: The Wasted Wink

items.text: Alex (would change): I would make the dawn reports or day logs say who visited whom, so claims about nest changes could be checked more easily.
items.title: The Wasted Wink

items.text: Blair (would change): I would make the confused-report rule clearer, so players know exactly what a confused dawn report looks like and can flag it cleanly.
items.title: The Wasted Wink

items.text: Casey (would change): Dawn reports could name each visitor's animal when an egg is gained or lost, so players could check claims without guessing.
items.title: The Wasted Wink

items.text: Drew (would change): Include each visitor's identity in the dawn report so egg-count claims can be checked directly.
items.title: The Wasted Wink

items.text: Ellis (would change): I would make the dawn reports clearer about who visited you, so confusion does not hide the truth from honest Farm players.
items.title: The Wasted Wink

items.text: Finley (would change): I'd make it clearer when a dawn report is confused, so players know whether a claim is unreliable.
items.title: The Wasted Wink

items.text: Alex, round 1: Her day statement was muddled. Casey had to correct that Casey visited Blair, not Alex.
items.title: The Wasted Wink

items.text: Blair's 15-point round-1 win came from a single secret. A lone Meowfia who knows a Farm role can throw at a player who is surely Farm. High throws from the winning side make one round decisive. Consider capping the pile value, or making the banked cards less decisive.
items.title: Blair Banks Big

items.text: Hugged and confused effects are invisible to the table, so valid reports looked like lies. Finley, Ellis, Blair and Drew all argued from egg counts that the hug had blanked. Fix: tell the hugged player at dawn that they were hugged.
items.title: Blair Banks Big

items.text: Meowfia don't know each other, so in round 2 both Meowfia threw at Casey, the same Farm player, and in round 3 Ellis threw at Finley while Alex threw at Casey. Meowfia play was mostly passive. Few deceptions had any bite. Consider giving Meowfia a way to find each other, or a stronger night action.
items.title: Blair Banks Big

items.text: Dead Blair still threw 0 for round 2 but banked high-value cards in round 3 and led by 30 points. After round 1 the game was effectively over. Add a catch-up rule, or scale the points per round.
items.title: Blair Banks Big

items.text: Alex (would change): Make the dawn reports clearer about who visited whom, so players can verify claims without rereading rules. Some counts were easy to misread under pressure.
items.title: Blair Banks Big

items.text: Casey (would change): Make the dawn reports clearer about which visitor or egg source caused each change, so players can check claims without guessing.
items.title: Blair Banks Big

items.text: Ellis (would change): Make the dawn reports clearer about who visited whom, so counting eggs against claims isn't guesswork.
items.title: Blair Banks Big

items.text: Setup bug: rounds 2 and 3 each dealt three Meowfia, which breaks the 'at most 2' rule. Players who reasoned correctly from the rule (Blair and Alex) were punished. Enforce the cap in the engine.
items.title: Three Cats, One Wink

items.text: Alex (confused by): The rules said at most 2 Meowfia, but rounds 2 and 3 each had three (me, Blair, Ellis, then me, Blair, Casey). Because I trusted that limit, I misread who my partners were and argued that Ellis's report was impossible.
items.title: Three Cats, One Wink

items.text: Blair (confused by): The rules say at most 2 Meowfia per round, but rounds 2 and 3 each had three. In round 2 I trusted the limit, decided Ellis must be Farm and attacked a teammate. It was also unclear at first that a double down only goes through when you win the floor.
items.title: Three Cats, One Wink

items.text: Blair (would change): Either enforce the 2-Meowfia cap or state the real limit. Hidden-team logic depends on the count, and a wrong count punishes careful deduction.
items.title: Three Cats, One Wink

items.text: Casey (would change): Have the Storyteller confirm each player's own nest count and clarify the Meowfia cap, since the rules and the hidden roles disagreed.
items.title: Three Cats, One Wink

items.text: Ellis (would change): Either enforce the cap on Meowfia or announce the possible counts, and give every animal in the pool a written description.
items.title: Three Cats, One Wink

items.text: Finley (would change): The cap on cats should be enforced as written, or the real number should be stated. Otherwise counting cats from egg changes and visitors, which is the core skill, is unreliable. I'd also make the handshake offers cost something, since cats used them freely to look trustworthy.
items.title: Three Cats, One Wink

items.text: Alex, round 2: Threw all 6 cards at Blair because Ellis's last message named her. His note assumed Ellis was also on Blair, but Ellis threw at Casey. That made the tie that lost the cats the round.
items.title: Three Cats, One Wink

items.text: Alex, round 3: Argued that Ellis's report meant three Meowfia, which the rules forbid. That was correct by the rules, but the engine had in fact dealt three.
items.title: Three Cats, One Wink

items.text: The engine log leaked 'no effect at tier 50' on the round 1 hug. Clean up internal debug text. Also, carried-over nests shrank to 2 cards for most players by round 3, so their only lever was the double down.
items.title: The Hawk Speaks Twice

items.text: Alex (would change): Let a special action like a wink or double-down happen even when you don't win the floor, as CAW CAW already does. Otherwise a key action can fail without you knowing.
items.title: The Hawk Speaks Twice

items.text: Blair (confused by): How double-down cards are entered was unclear. I first put them inside the special action, the schema rejected it, and they actually go in the top-level cards field. It was also easy to forget that my early double down still counted for score after I was winked, but not as a vote.
items.title: The Hawk Speaks Twice

items.text: Casey (would change): I would make the public nest-size list reflect only real egg-laying, not draws caused by confusion, or at least flag the confusion rule more clearly. As it stands, nest changes can quietly back up a false claim.
items.title: The Hawk Speaks Twice

items.text: Drew (confused by): In round 1 I lost several bids, so my visit to Alex was never actually said. I then doubled down as if the table already knew it. It wasn't obvious that words I wrote but didn't get to say counted for nothing.
items.title: The Hawk Speaks Twice

items.text: Drew (would change): Have the app confirm which claims and details each player has actually said aloud, so players don't assume information was shared when it wasn't.
items.title: The Hawk Speaks Twice

items.text: Ellis (confused by): The timing of double-down wasn't clear. My first attempt silently didn't happen because I didn't win the floor, even though the special-action wording read as if it would act right away. It was also unclear whether a dead player's thrown cards count as votes against them until it played out.
items.title: The Hawk Speaks Twice

items.text: Ellis (would change): Let a double-down or other special action happen even when you don't win the floor, like CAW CAW does. Tying it to winning the bid makes the 'before you have spoken' window feel random.
items.title: The Hawk Speaks Twice

items.text: Finley (would change): Show each player their running score and the bonus breakdown after every round, not just at the start of the next one. That would make the trade-off between doubling down and bonding easier to judge.
items.title: The Hawk Speaks Twice

items.text: Runaway leader: one doubled win in round 2 put Blair out of reach. Round 3 became a vote against the leader, not a deduction, and Blair won the game after losing two of three rounds. Fix: drop or reduce doubling in the last round, or score rounds on placement.
items.title: The Mouser's Three Winks

items.text: Clarity of the log and payouts: 'won, 29 points' showed the base value while the total added 58, and 'no effect at tier 50' is engine jargon. Show the doubled bonus and the bond changes in plain words.
items.title: The Mouser's Three Winks

items.text: Alex (confused by): Special actions like the wink only happen if you win the floor. Several of my wink attempts silently did nothing, and I couldn't be sure the timing would land before the vote.
items.title: The Mouser's Three Winks

items.text: Alex (would change): Let dead players' thrown cards still count as votes, or make the wink cost something. Right now a wink that cancels a public double-down is very strong.
items.title: The Mouser's Three Winks

items.text: Casey (confused by): A special action only happens if you win the floor. That cost me in round 2: my double-down kept not going through, and when it finally did I was winked straight away, so my 4 votes didn't count. It also wasn't clear at first that dead players' thrown cards score but don't count as votes.
items.title: The Mouser's Three Winks

items.text: Casey (would change): Make it clear that a special action happens only if you win the floor, maybe by letting double-downs go through right away like CAW CAW. As it is, the timing feels random.
items.title: The Mouser's Three Winks

items.text: Ellis (confused by): How double-down works in the reply format. I first put the cards inside the special action and got a schema error, so the right place for them wasn't clear. It also wasn't obvious how the "bonus" points shown in the final scores are made up.
items.title: The Mouser's Three Winks

items.text: Finley (confused by): In round 3, Blair said doubling down only staked a Wild, a 1 and a 5. That made me unsure how much the double-down bonus really mattered in the standings. The note that winks are anonymous was clear enough, but it made it hard to tell who to suspect after each death.
items.title: The Mouser's Three Winks

items.text: Finley (would change): Double-downs fix votes early, so whoever commits first with the most cards often decides the vote before the facts come out. I'd stop doubled cards from counting as votes until the eggsecution, or cap how many cards a double-down can throw.
items.title: The Mouser's Three Winks

items.text: Ellis, round 3: Shook Alex's hand on the strength of a role claim that couldn't be checked, and took -3 from a cross-alignment bond.
items.title: The Mouser's Three Winks

items.text: Setup bug: rounds 2 and 3 each dealt 3 Meowfia (Alex, Blair, Ellis; then Alex, Blair, Casey), breaking the 'at most 2' rule. It decided round 2, because true information was rejected as impossible. Enforce the cap in the engine.
items.title: The Third Cat

items.text: Alex (confused by): The rules say at most 2 Meowfia, yet rounds 2 and 3 each had three cats (Alex, Blair, Ellis, then Alex, Blair, Casey). So Finley's 'three cats on Drew' report was true, and I helped get Finley eggsecuted by calling it impossible. It was also unclear that special actions like double down only happen if you win the floor.
items.title: The Third Cat

items.text: Alex (would change): Either enforce the 2-Meowfia cap or state clearly that it can be broken. Players reason from that rule, and it decided round 2. I'd also let a declared special action go through even when the player doesn't win the floor.
items.title: The Third Cat

items.text: Blair (would change): Make sure the setup follows the stated Meowfia cap, or drop the cap from the rules, and give every animal in the pool a description. Players can only reason well if the rules match what the game actually does.
items.title: The Third Cat

items.text: Drew (would change): The alignment cap should match what actually happens. If three cats can show up, the rules should say so, because players use the cap to catch lies.
items.title: The Third Cat

items.text: Ellis (confused by): The rules said at most 2 Meowfia per round, but rounds 2 and 3 each had 3. In round 2 I argued Finley's three-cat report was impossible, and it turned out to be true. A hard limit that isn't enforced makes rules-based deduction misleading.
items.title: The Third Cat

items.text: Ellis (would change): Either enforce the Meowfia cap or state clearly that it can be exceeded. Also, a dead player's thrown cards still leave their nest but count for nothing, which makes the wink feel very swingy.
items.title: The Third Cat

items.text: Ellis, round 2: Called Finley's report impossible because at most 2 players are Meowfia. That was correct by the written rules, but the engine had dealt 3 cats, so the rules misled the whole table.
items.title: The Third Cat

items.text: Alex, round 2: Said 'three cats can't exist' while being the third cat himself. The rules text and the real deal disagreed.
items.title: The Third Cat

items.text: The day ends too fast and alignment repeats. Both days ended at beat 2 on unanimous CAWs, Drew was Meowfia twice, and his score of 9 left him nothing to play for. Also, Casey's line appeared after the day had ended, which looks like an app ordering bug. Fix: require a minimum number of beats before CAW counts, and avoid giving the same player Meowfia in back-to-back rounds.
items.title: The Eagle's Big Nest

items.text: Alex (confused by): Nothing major; the bonus scoring wasn't obvious at first, and my round 1 egg draws before the first night (3 to 5 cards) caught me briefly off guard.
items.title: The Eagle's Big Nest

items.text: Blair (confused by): How the final score counts the pile and the nest. Alex's 10-card throw showed that nest size and throw volume matter a lot, and that wasn't obvious up front.
items.title: The Eagle's Big Nest

items.text: Blair (would change): Give players a bit more information about how the bonus and the egg-gain mechanics play out. As it was, one player drawing 5 eggs let them overtake everyone.
items.title: The Eagle's Big Nest

items.text: Casey (confused by): How the bonus and the throw economy interact: Alex threw 10 cards and banked 65 points, and I didn't see how much hand size and the Wattle bond decided the outcome.
items.title: The Eagle's Big Nest

items.text: Casey (would change): Show the hand-size changes more clearly, or cap how many eggs one player can gain from a night's visits, since Alex's big nest made him run away with the game.
items.title: The Eagle's Big Nest

items.text: Drew (confused by): Nest sizes being public made egg-count lies easy to catch, and it wasn't obvious how much my own draw count would give me away.
items.title: The Eagle's Big Nest

items.text: Ellis (confused by): How Alex's nest jumped to 11 and how the 5-egg cap and nest sizes interact with claims; also that throwing a whole nest scores so much more than keeping cards.
items.title: The Eagle's Big Nest

items.text: Blair, round 2: Said Alex gained 5 eggs. Alex gained 4: he had 5 cards, drew 2 at setup and got 4 at night. Casey and Drew repeated the 5.
items.title: The Eagle's Big Nest

items.text: Blair, round 2: Claimed Drew should have 5 cards, so his 6 meant hidden eggs. Drew had 4 after round 1, drew 2 at setup and gained none, so 6 was correct. The 2-card setup draw was forgotten.
items.title: The Eagle's Big Nest

items.text: Finley, round 2: Repeated Blair's wrong nest math as evidence against Drew.
items.title: The Eagle's Big Nest

items.text: A one-round game makes the scoring meaningless. Whoever is Meowfia on a 1-Meowfia roll nearly wins by default, and the score announcements and the 'outscore your teammates' tension never come up. Play 3+ rounds.
items.title: The Pigeon Who Wasn't

items.text: Drew, round 1: Threw everything thinking 'if we lose, my highest card comes back.' The consolation only applies if you threw at the other team. If Gray turned out Farm, Drew had thrown at his own team and got nothing back.
items.title: The Pigeon Who Wasn't

items.text: Alex, round 1: Called CAW CAW in speech and then again. It's unclear if the first call counted, since the clock had just been reset by the extension.
items.title: The Pigeon Who Wasn't

items.text: A lone cat who joins the bandwagon banks every card it throws. The result was 37 to 5 in a one-round game. Consider capping the cat's payout or scaling it by the number of Meowfia. As it stands, one wrong vote decides the whole game.
items.title: The Phantom Pigeon Egg

items.text: Gray, round 1: Gray kept S8 in the throw because it 'comes back if we lose'. That can't happen: Farm only loses here if Blair is Farm, and throwing at your own team gets no consolation card.
items.title: The Phantom Pigeon Egg

items.text: Finley, round 1: Finley said 'I can't offer again this round.' No rule limits handshake offers.
items.title: The Phantom Pigeon Egg

items.text: Ellis, round 1: Ellis kept C1 because it is 'worth more kept'. A 1 is worth 1 whether you keep it or bank it.
items.title: The Phantom Pigeon Egg

items.text: Nests carry over between rounds, but the day listing shows only raw sizes. Four players took leftover cards for night eggs. Show each nest's change since the round's deal.
items.title: Two Tits, Two Owls

items.text: The Wink was weak. Casey died but still banked 37 points. Drew was eggsecuted anyway, and the kill made him look guilty. Consider making dead players' throws not score, or using the Wink before throws are locked.
items.title: Two Tits, Two Owls

items.text: Which team you got decided the winner. Finley was Meowfia twice and scored 7. Alex was Farm twice, had a 13 to throw, and won. With only 2 rounds and a one-card consolation for the losers, being Meowfia is close to an automatic loss. Also, players in the same group could speak after the CAW, so Finley's best evidence arrived after the day had ended.
items.title: Two Tits, Two Owls

items.text: Alex, round 2: Called Finley's 7 cards suspicious, but those were cards left over from Round 1.
items.title: Two Tits, Two Owls

items.text: Blair, round 2: Asked who visited Finley because Finley had 7 cards. That was leftover cards, not night eggs.
items.title: Two Tits, Two Owls

items.text: Casey, round 2: Also called Finley's 7 cards odd when they were just leftover cards.
items.title: Two Tits, Two Owls

items.text: Confusion is very swingy. In round 1 the random wrong role matched the cat's bluff exactly and decided the round. Casey also discarded a real card for a fake egg loss. A false report that also costs a real card feels harsh.
items.title: The Honest Kookaburra

items.text: Hugs are invisible to the hugged player, but confusion is announced. Round 2 turned on whether Alex's blank report was real. Consider telling hugged players they were hugged, or make the gap a deliberate rule.
items.title: The Honest Kookaburra

items.text: Scoring favours keeping high cards for later rounds. Alex threw everything in round 1 and finished on 4. Drew held his 12 and 13 and later banked 41 with them. Nests shrink to 2-4 cards after round 1, so the first round's throws carry far more weight than later ones.
items.title: The Honest Kookaburra

items.text: Nest sizes carry over between rounds, and the Round 1 consolation card changes them. Together these make it very hard to work out who gained eggs. That one math error decided Round 2. Have the Storyteller list each nest's size at the start of the night as well as at dawn.
items.title: The Missing Eight

items.text: The pool already held every animal at the start of Round 1, and the reveal turned up the same flower twice. So the per-round reveal added nothing. Check whether this is intended or a bug in the deck.
items.title: The Missing Eight

items.text: Throw sizes swing votes heavily. Drew's 7-card nest gave him the decisive 5 votes, while Finley threw everything in Round 1 and started Round 2 with only 2 cards. A round-one pile-on gives no-risk points (Casey banked 45). Round 2 was the only real contest.
items.title: The Missing Eight

items.text: Blair, round 2: Read the new nest sizes as egg gains and losses ('Alex and Finley lost eggs, Drew and Casey gained'), but nest sizes carry over between rounds.
items.title: The Missing Eight

items.text: Ellis, round 2: Made the same mistake ('Drew +3, Finley -2, Alex -1'). His corrected baseline for Drew (4 kept + 2 drawn = 6) also missed the S8 returned to Drew in Round 1.
items.title: The Missing Eight

items.text: Blair, round 2: Repeated Ellis's wrong baseline of 6 for Drew and voted on it.
items.title: The Missing Eight

items.text: Casey, round 2: Private reasoning said 'visit Drew', but Casey's night choice was Ellis.
items.title: The Missing Eight

items.text: Blair, round 1: Threw all 5 cards at Alex, hoping for a tie, when Drew was clearly going to lose the vote. Only H12 came back, so Blair ended on 1 point instead of a safe 5. This is a strategy error, not a rule misread.
items.title: Three Blank Visits

items.text: Ellis, round 1: Was confident about Drew and called CAW, but threw only W2 (worth 0). He banked nothing from a winning vote and finished on 4. No reasoning was recorded, so this may be a misunderstanding of how throwing pays.
items.title: Three Blank Visits

items.text: A winning team banks every thrown card, even cards thrown at a teammate. Finley threw at Farm Drew and still banked 12. This weakens the reason to work out the right target. You could bank only cards thrown at the player who was eggsecuted, or only cards thrown at the other team.
items.title: Egg Math Catches Cats

items.text: Ellis, round 2: He said Casey's 5-card nest was her starting size. Casey had started the night at 4.
items.title: Egg Math Catches Cats

items.text: Ellis, round 2: He assumed Casey's visit had confused him. Blair was the one who visited him; Casey visited Finley.
items.title: Egg Math Catches Cats

items.text: No-Meowfia rounds happen about 9% of the time ((2/3)^6), and they wiped out round 1 completely. Nobody even considered the possibility, so the game came down to one round. Consider giving a small hint, or letting an all-Farm table win if the vote is spread out.
items.title: The Empty Barn

items.text: Ellis, round 1: Called Casey's Drew visit 'shaky' even though Drew's and Casey's egg reports matched exactly.
items.title: The Empty Barn

items.text: Ellis, round 2: Said 'Confirmed again', but it was Ellis's first confirmation.
items.title: The Empty Barn

items.text: Casey, round 2: Used Ellis's round 1 role as evidence, even though roles are re-dealt every round.
items.title: The Empty Barn

items.text: Confused players really draw cards for phantom eggs. Casey got S10 and S12 (22 points) from a false report and banked them. Decide whether confusion should cost or pay real cards. Right now it is a windfall. The log line 'hugged: no effect at tier 50' is also unclear. Casey's report never said she was hugged or that she learned no role.
items.title: Sphinx Caught Twice

items.text: Meowfia never won, so the two cat players ended with 4–5 points and the Farm players with 38–61. Over 2 rounds, a player who rolls Meowfia twice has no route back. Consider more rounds, or a better consolation for the losing side.
items.title: Sphinx Caught Twice

items.text: Drew, round 2: Said Alex 'lost 2 eggs'. Alex's nest was 3 because he threw 4 cards in round 1 and drew 2 at setup. No eggs were stolen.
items.title: Sphinx Caught Twice

items.text: Casey, round 1: Blamed the confusion only on Finley's visit. Drew and Blair visited too.
items.title: The Lucky Pigeon Lie

items.text: Finley, round 2: Thought nests started the round at 4 and called Ellis's 6 cards and Alex's 3 suspicious. Players draw 2 on top of whatever they kept.
items.title: The Lucky Pigeon Lie

items.text: Blair, round 2: Accused Ellis over the same wrong nest math (6 cards but 'no eggs').
items.title: The Lucky Pigeon Lie

items.text: Alex, round 2: Was Meowfia and noted that any Farm eggsecution would win it for him, then threw at Drew, his fellow Meowfia. He lost both cards.
items.title: The Lucky Pigeon Lie

items.text: Drew, round 3: Called Blair's nest of 3 odd when nothing changed. That is normal carry-over (1 kept + 2 drawn). Finley repeated it.
items.title: The Lucky Pigeon Lie

items.text: Finley, round 3: His reasoning said 'visit Alex' but he chose Casey.
items.title: The Lucky Pigeon Lie

items.text: Consolation cards show up in public nest sizes, so anyone counting cards can see who was Meowfia last round. That decided round 2 with no evidence from the night. Consider returning the card face-down into the score pile instead of the nest.
items.title: Blair, Cat Three Times

items.text: The 64-card deck ran out in round 3. Gains then stopped showing in nest sizes, which removed the main evidence. Reshuffle discards, or shrink the hand sizes.
items.title: Blair, Cat Three Times

items.text: Drew, round 1: Repeated the same mistake: 'Blair and Finley's eggs can't both vanish on Alex.'
items.title: Blair, Cat Three Times

items.text: Finley, round 2: Counted nests from the round 1 throws without adding consolation cards, and wrongly said Ellis and Blair had each gained an egg.
items.title: Blair, Cat Three Times

items.text: Finley, round 3: Accused Ellis of copying his claim. They had spoken in the same turn group, so Ellis could not have seen it.
items.title: Blair, Cat Three Times

items.text: Blair, round 3: Said 'nobody else moved' except Alex. Drew had gained 2 eggs, but the deck was empty, so his nest didn't grow.
items.title: Blair, Cat Three Times

items.text: Scoring ignores accuracy when your team wins. Casey threw 4 cards at a Farm teammate and banked 27. Combined with round 1's two-cat win (46 banked), an early round can decide the game. Blair's lead from round 1 was never caught.
items.title: The Silent Floofer Hug

items.text: Ellis, round 2: Worked out nest changes from a baseline of 5 for everyone. Nests carry over between rounds.
items.title: The Silent Floofer Hug

items.text: Blair, round 3: Said Alex was '+3' from a baseline of 5, but Alex had carried 6 cards over and drawn 2.
items.title: The Silent Floofer Hug

items.text: Alex, round 2: Miscounted Ellis's nest by forgetting the consolation card returned in round 1, and accused Ellis of hiding a +1.
items.title: Unseen Hugs

items.text: Drew, round 2: Made the same counting error: forgot the returned cards and said Blair was +2 and Ellis +1, when Blair was +1 and Ellis +0.
items.title: Unseen Hugs

items.text: Ellis, round 2: Said Alex and Blair were both +2. Alex was unchanged and Blair was +1.
items.title: Unseen Hugs

items.text: Winks were a strong private oracle. Winking someone on the other side draws 2 eggs, so Alex knew Casey's and Blair's sides for certain. Nest sizes are only listed at dawn, so he could not prove it. In round 1 the Lorikeet handed out five Winks, and the instant kill silenced Casey, the only player who could explain the egg count.
items.title: Swaps and Confessions

items.text: Throws were flat: nearly everyone threw their two highest cards at the consensus target. The one big swing came from round 1's wrong vote, which made a dead Casey the eventual winner. Allowing larger throws, or rewarding a lone correct dissent, could create more betting tension.
items.title: Swaps and Confessions

items.text: Drew, round 1: Called the fourth egg 'odd' and threw at Alex. Did not see that the Lorikeet egg explained it.
items.title: Swaps and Confessions

items.text: The deck ran out by round 3. Laid eggs then showed as +0 on the public change list, while private reports still said an egg was laid. This erased the main evidence and caused the Farm loss. Add a reshuffle, a bigger deck, or a public count of eggs laid. Casey's report also printed a blank card ("You drew ."), and the nest-size line was printed twice.
items.title: The Top Cat Flips

items.text: Six Winks were handed out, and nobody ever used one. The Lorikeet only worked as a way to confirm a role. Winks need a reason to be used, or a cost for not using them.
items.title: The Top Cat Flips

items.text: Card values decide too much. Ellis's single throw of 12, 13 and 13 in round 1 (38 points) was the winning margin by itself. Every vote was a near-unanimous pile-on, so the betting rarely added any tension.
items.title: The Top Cat Flips

items.text: Casey, round 1: As a flipped Meowfia, rated Alex 75% likely Meowfia, then threw at him anyway. A throw at your own teammate loses and gets no card back.
items.title: The Top Cat Flips

items.text: Drew, round 2: Threw at Ellis believing Ellis was Farm, to get a card back if he lost. Ellis was a Meowfia teammate, so no card came back.

items.text: Score growth makes the last round decide the game. Nests grow, so round 3 throws dwarf everything earlier: 94 points from one throw against 18 from a whole round-1 win. Consider capping banked cards or scaling earlier rounds.
items.title: Two Maine Coons Bust

items.text: Casey, round 3: Casey claimed that throwing at Alex 'may decide nothing' because Alex was already dead from a failed Coon bet. Ellis and Finley said it was a guaranteed win. The rules don't say whether a player who lost exclusively can be eggsecuted, or what that would mean for Farm, so nobody could settle it.
items.title: Two Maine Coons Bust

items.text: Drew, round 3: Drew planned to throw one high card for the consolation and then threw all 8 cards into a vote he expected to lose. He dropped from 8 points to 1, so he seemed to underrate how expensive losing throws are.
items.title: Two Maine Coons Bust

items.text: In a one-round game, losing on your own team costs everything thrown. Ellis lost 43 points and Blair won by 33. A single misread vote decides the whole game. Consider playing more rounds, or giving a small floor for losers.

items.title: Cats Egg Their Own

items.text: Round 1 was a dead round. With no Meowfia, the table proved it by beat 2, everyone threw a Wild, and Alex was eliminated at random. Rounds with zero cats need either rarer odds or some payoff for correctly calling 'no cat'. As it stands the only skill is throwing your cheapest card.
items.title: A Busted Cat Comes Back

items.text: A confused report has real effects: Casey drew 3 cards when her true gain was +1, and Ellis drew 1 when his was 0. Confusing someone can make their hand bigger, and Casey turned those extra cards into votes. On top of that, cards kept after a lost round become ammunition later, which is why the caught round-2 cat tied for first. That may be intended, but it means caught cats are barely punished.

changes.title: Confidence tokens (6.3)
changes.setting: vote.weight=player vote.max_throw=3 vote.min_throw=0 scoring.payout=read game.announce_scores=false vote.confidence=true
changes.hypothesis: Confidence tokens create a real sizing decision without letting one round decide the game
changes.against_package: Against the scoring package on the same seeds: best-round share 54% to 59% (worse), alignment neutrality 1.88 to 1.34, side share 41% to 34%, card luck 49% to 45% (interval -9.5 to +1 pts). A sizing decision that evens the sides but lets one round matter more. Verdict on best round against the package: reject.

changes.title: Banded card values (6.3)
changes.setting: vote.weight=player vote.max_throw=3 vote.min_throw=0 scoring.payout=read game.announce_scores=false scoring.values="banded"
changes.hypothesis: Card values decide less: fewer winners change when banked cards are re-scored at the average
changes.against_package: Against the scoring package on the same seeds: card-luck sensitivity 49% to 48% (interval -6 to +3.5 pts), best-round share 54% to 46%, accuracy share +2 pts, hoarder 2% to 5.5%. Banding narrows the spread of card values too little to change many winners. Verdict on card luck: reject.

changes.title: Tell a hugged player (6.8)
changes.hypothesis: Fewer honest Farm players are eggsecuted because of a hug they were not told about

changes.title: Egg tokens, cashed after the vote (6.6)
changes.hypothesis: The table reads the round better when nest counts are exact and confusion moves no cards

changes.title: Open vote, trial, then stake (6.5)
changes.hypothesis: A real choice between two: more candidates share the vote; the tension score rises

changes.title: The cats see each other, with safe claims (6.4)
changes.hypothesis: Cats who know each other stop hitting each other; Farm wins less

changes.title: The scoring package (6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.7)
changes.hypothesis: The scoring package: the hoarding exploiter no longer wins far above its share

changes.title: Secret score piles (6.7)
changes.hypothesis: Nobody can vote against the leader: the leader-hunting exploiter wins less

changes.title: A stake of at most three cards (6.3)
changes.hypothesis: No single round outweighs the others: the winner gets less of the score from their best round

changes.title: The stake pays on your own read (6.2)
changes.hypothesis: A correct read is paid: accuracy explains more of a winner points; the sides even out
changes.tuning: On top of one vote each and the three-card cap, 100 paired scripted seeds per point. Meowfia multiple 1: alignment neutrality 0.97 to 1.02, accuracy share 27 to 29%, best-round share 46 to 48%. Multiple 2: neutrality about 2.0, accuracy about 20%, best round 52 to 53%. The side bonus (0, 5, 10) barely matters. Scripted cats lie better than Claude cats, so Claude tables may need a higher multiple.

changes.title: One player, one vote (6.1)
changes.hypothesis: Largest single share of the vote falls; fewer rounds decided by one throw

changes.title: Nest sizes show their change
changes.detail: The day's list of nest sizes gives each nest's change since this round's deal, because nests carry over between rounds and players were reading leftover cards as last night's eggs.

changes.title: Golden Wattle: answer at once
changes.detail: A player offered a handshake must accept or decline there and then.

changes.title: The Goose needs a player
changes.detail: Scoring is inverted only when a player is the Goose; each Goose inverts it once.

changes.title: The pool is the chosen cards
changes.detail: Every chosen animal is in the pool from round one; nothing is revealed during the game. A set number of the chosen flowers are picked at random and stay all game unless their card says to discard them.

changes.title: First place is the goal
changes.detail: The rules say only first place wins and spell out the pull between team and self. Scores are announced at the start of each round. A seat can be given a temperament.

changes.title: Crimson Kunzea: the early vote
changes.detail: Doubling down means throwing your eggs at a player there and then, in the open, as your vote.

changes.title: Meowfia count by table size
changes.detail: 1 Meowfia at four players, 1 or 2 at five or six, 2 or 3 at seven or eight, instead of a 33% roll. Messages over the word limit end at a full sentence.

changes.title: Live talk: word clock and exchanges
changes.detail: The day is a clock of spoken words, messages are short, two players can go back and forth, and CAW CAW counts without the floor.

changes.title: Live talk: bidding for the floor
changes.detail: After every message each player bids 0 to 3 to speak next; naming a player favours them.

changes.title: Live talk and the basics setup
changes.detail: A second discussion system, live talk, and a basics-only setup for testing.

changes.title: Golden Wattle explains its payoff
changes.detail: The turn prompt says what a bond pays.

changes.title: One game with settings
changes.detail: The separate v9, v10 and dusk variants were folded into one game with settings.

changes.title: Dusk and a set number of Meowfia
changes.detail: A talk phase before every night became possible, and the number of Meowfia could be set instead of rolled.
